content_txt: Total self-indulgence from the director. It’s the same old story wrapped in a 'fantasy' skin. Loved this movie about what happens after you die. Interesting take: When you pass away & are sent to the afterlife, you physically become the age/appearance you were when you were happiest in life. In this world it is surprisingly corporate: there are diff eternities & they have salespeople who try to sell you the eternity. You can choose 1 eternity to live in but you cant reverse your decision: food world, museum world, beach world, mountain world, bromance world, workout world etc. Or you can stay in limbo if you can't decide if you get a job. Joan sees both of her past husbands in the afterlife: a young love who has waited 60 years in limbo for her & her most recent hubby of many years.She has to choose who to spend eternity with. At 1 point she goes w/ her girl friend, then chooses young love but realizes it's shallow & she can't forget memories of her entire life so she takes a risk, escapes & chooses latest hubby. They choose the eternity of the town they lived in: Oakdale world

Even the choice framed as "choosing herself" had her following someone else into their afterlife, and even that choice didn’t stick. I LOVE the casting choice of Miles Teller and Elizabeth Olsen in Eternity. This movie stayed with me in a way few films do. It’s one of those stories that quietly changes your perspective and lingers in your thoughts long after it ends. Joan feels painfully human. She’s torn between love, regret, and fear of choosing wrong. Larry represents steady, unconditional love, the kind that shows up every day and asks for nothing but honesty. That’s why I loved him so much, and why it hurt so deeply when Joan slept with Luke. It felt unfair to Larry, and it broke my heart. But it also showed how complicated love really is, and how even good people make choices that come from confusion and longing. This movie made me laugh, made me cry, and left me emotionally shaken. Eternity isn’t just about romance. It’s about choice, timing, and the weight of loving someone deeply. By the end, I felt sad, full, and strangely hopeful all at once. That’s what makes this movie unforgettable.

I get the romance part; however, the attempted comedy was very flat and signaled by the actor's raised voices and animated expressions. Fine. The performances were capable enough, given the material they were working with. Yet, these are assuredly not improvisational actors, so therefore, no chances of saving the script from itself. The story was expectedly, predictably twisty (will she/won’t she choose one or the other), but eventually it turned sweet as the Olsen's Joan reflected on her life experiences and choices. Such nostalgia wrung a bit of sweetness by the end. "I’m happy when you’re happy..." said her husband Larry (Miles Teller). I could have (and should have) waited to watch on streaming, and I would have been happier. However, I’m doing my part to support cinema with limited theatrical offerings here in the Midwest, where "culture" is more commonly referred to as "mildew in the bathtub."

Eternity is a sweet and entertaining film. It's a clever film with a unique construct, that mostly works. The film is a fantasy romantic comedy. It begins with elderly Larry and Joan on the way to a family gender reveal. When Larry chokes on peanuts he dies and 'wakes up' in the 'The Junction', the place that dead people frequent before they decide which Afterlife world they will inhabit. But he discovers that Luke is also there. Luke was Joan's first husband before he was killed in the Korean War. When Joan passes, she joins them there and it's a battle for her affection. Who does she want to spend her afterlife with? Her first love or her husband of 50 years. So ensues a fairly reliable comedy that works because of the leads in Elizabeth Olsen, Miles Teller and Callum Turner. It's a bright and fun film, but it also manages to have its moving moments as the film works towards its conclusion. A solid and reliable film that manages to provide enjoyable entertainment.

Austin Film Festival Screening #6:

Though the premise is one that feels familiar, Eternity is the latest A24 film to succeed in delivering compelling characters of depth and an unapologetically emotional premise. Directed by David Freyne, Eternity builds a story around the concept of what happens to one’s soul after death. Constructing multiple romances that feel genuine, it’s actually the comedy of Eternity that left me impressed. Though the plot of the film is extremely simple, it’s the performances of Eternity that elevate this script and screenplay. 

Miles Teller, Elizabeth Olsen, and Callum Turner are a talented trio whose performances capture a charm and playfulness. While these three truly showcase their talent throughout Eternity, it’s the supporting performance from Da’Vine Joy Randolph that’s my favorite. From the film’s opening act, there is no secret to the direction that Eternity is heading. In fact, it’s the predictability of the film that makes it slightly less exciting or interesting. Of all the films I have seen at Austin Film Festival, Eternity is the definitely the most accessible and straightforward. 

Overall, Eternity doesn’t deliver too many surprises but the film never feels boring or repetitive. Elizabeth Olsen is genuinely so good in the role and her chemistry with Miles Teller and Callum Turner feels genuine. A fantastical glimpse into love, devotion, and commitment, Eternity delivers constant laughs from every character.

David Freyne’s “Eternity” is a delightful and heartwarming film starring Miles Teller, Elizabeth Olsen, and Callum Turner, that presents an amusing narrative about a deceased woman at a post-life waystation who must choose between her two husbands.

In an afterlife where souls have a week to decide their eternal destination, Joan (Elizabeth Olsen) faces the impossible decision between her life partner (Miles Teller) and her first love (Callum Turner), who has waited decades for her arrival.

Despite feeling more like a play at times and a little predictable, this romantic comedy captivates with its creative and ever-evolving afterlife. The film remains light-hearted and humorous, yet deeply moving, encouraging viewers to find paradise in the present and cherish those we love.

Overall, “Eternity” is a beautifully crafted and entertaining world that unfolds parallel to a captivating love triangle story. Each character delivers a standout performance, particularly Elizabeth Olsen. It’s a delightful cinematic experience, with a good message. Despite feeling small, this is one of the purest and sweetest movies you’ll encounter this year. ⭐️⭐️⭐️

I recently watched Eternity, and I was genuinely surprised by how much it stuck with me after the credits rolled. It’s one of those movies that starts off slow and subtle, but before you know it, you’re completely pulled into its world. The film balances emotion, mystery, and visual storytelling in a way that feels thoughtful rather than forced, and by the end, it felt like I had gone through an entire journey with the characters.

One of the strongest parts of Eternity is the atmosphere. The cinematography is beautiful—every frame feels intentional, with lighting and scenery that match the emotional tone of each scene. Whether it’s a quiet moment between characters or a dramatic turning point, the visuals always enhance what’s happening instead of distracting from it.

The acting was another highlight. Every character felt believable, and the performances had real depth. Even the smaller roles added something meaningful to the story. The lead actor especially stood out, bringing a mix of vulnerability, strength, and complexity that made the character feel truly human. You can tell the cast fully committed to their roles.
